name: Combed Cotton Poplin 120
summary: A 120 gsm combed cotton poplin with a smooth, crisp hand — our most-ordered shirting base, OEKO-TEX certified and available in 40 stock colours from 100 m.
description: Combed cotton poplin 120 is a plain-weave shirting fabric woven from combed, ring-spun 60s yarns. Combing removes short fibres, which gives the cloth its clean surface, low pilling and the crisp hand that presses well and holds a collar.

It is piece-dyed with reactive dyes to 4–5 wash fastness, then sanforised so residual shrinkage stays under 2%. Typical uses are dress shirts, blouses and uniform shirting; for a softer, more casual handle choose the 110 gsm version and ask for an enzyme wash.
imageAlt: Macro detail of crisp white combed cotton poplin fabric

faqs.question: What is combed cotton poplin used for?
faqs.answer: It is used mainly for dress shirts, blouses and uniform shirting because the combed yarn gives a smooth, pill-resistant surface that presses crisply and takes a sharp collar.

faqs.question: How much does 120 gsm poplin cost?
faqs.answer: Indicative pricing is US$1.65–2.20 per metre FOB Shanghai at 3,000 metres, depending on shade depth and finish. Stock colours sit at the lower end; custom lab dips add a one-off matching fee.

name: Cotton Twill 240
summary: A 240 gsm cotton twill with a 3/1 diagonal face for chinos, uniforms and light jackets, available in piece-dyed and garment-dyed finishes from 300 m.
description: This 3/1 twill is woven from 20s warp and 16s weft cotton, giving a firm diagonal face and enough body for trousers without the stiffness of canvas. It is the construction most chino programmes settle on after testing 220–260 gsm.

We finish it with a compressive shrinkage pass, then calender lightly. For garment dyeing we supply it in greige or semi-bleached with a dye recipe matched to your wash house, and we can pre-test for the shade shift your laundry expects.
finish: Piece dyed or greige for garment dyeing
imageAlt: Macro detail of khaki cotton twill fabric showing diagonal ribs

faqs.question: Can this twill be garment dyed?
faqs.answer: Yes. We supply it greige or semi-bleached with a documented recipe, and we can pre-test the shade shift your laundry will see so the bulk wash result is predictable.

faqs.question: Is 240 gsm heavy enough for trousers?
faqs.answer: For chinos and uniform trousers, yes. For jeans-style five-pocket construction most brands move up to 280–320 gsm or switch to denim for better seam strength.

name: Cotton Canvas 320
summary: A 320 gsm 2/1 cotton canvas for bags, workwear and structured jackets, with high tear strength and optional water-repellent finish, from 500 m.
description: Our 320 gsm canvas is a 2/1 basket-weave construction built from 10s and 7s cotton yarns. It is dense, dimensionally stable and holds a structured shape, which is why bag makers and workwear brands specify it over twill.

Standard finish is a wash-and-wear softening pass; for bags we recommend a paraffin or C0 water-repellent finish which raises the spray rating to 4 without changing the hand. Tear strength is tested to ASTM D1424 and reported per lot.
features: High tear strength for bag construction
ASTM D1424 tear report per lot
imageAlt: Macro detail of natural heavy cotton canvas with basket weave

faqs.question: What is canvas used for in apparel?
faqs.answer: In apparel it is used for structured jackets, workwear trousers, aprons and chore coats. Outside apparel it is the standard base for tote bags, tool bags and home accessories because of its tear strength.

faqs.question: Can canvas be printed?
faqs.answer: Yes, but screen printing on 320 gsm canvas needs a thicker ink deposit. Many bag brands prefer pigment printing or embroidery; we can supply a print trial length before bulk.

name: Washed Linen 180
summary: A 180 gsm European flax linen, garment-washed for a soft, lived-in hand, pre-shrunk to under 3% and OEKO-TEX certified — our best seller for resort and Gulf markets.
description: Woven from 100% certified European flax, this 180 gsm plain-weave linen is garment-washed in soft water without harsh enzymes, so the fibre keeps its strength while the surface softens. The result is the dry, cool hand customers expect from linen at first wear, not after a season.

Because linen is the most requested fabric in hot, humid climates, we grade each lot for evenness and residual shrinkage. Width is a consistent 145 cm with a tight ±2 cm tolerance, which keeps your marker efficiency predictable across repeat orders.
features: Soft washed hand from first wear
imageAlt: Macro detail of washed oatmeal linen with natural slubs

faqs.question: Is washed linen pre-shrunk?
faqs.answer: Yes. Our washed linen is pre-shrunk to under 3% residual shrinkage in both directions, and each bulk shipment ships with a shrinkage report from the finishing line.

faqs.question: Why is linen a good choice for hot climates?
faqs.answer: Linen fibres are hollow and highly moisture-absorbent, so they wick perspiration away and dry quickly while staying cool to the touch. It also drapes with coverage rather than clinging, which suits modest and resort silhouettes.

name: Linen Cotton Blend 160
summary: A 55/45 linen-cotton blend at 160 gsm that keeps the linen look with less creasing and a lower cost — a practical shirting and dress base from 300 m.
description: Blending 55% linen with 45% cotton softens the crease and lowers the price without losing the slub character buyers recognise as linen. At 160 gsm it is light enough for summer shirting and structured enough for dresses and wide-leg trousers.
The cotton content also improves dye uptake consistency, so pale and mid-tone shades repeat more closely than on 100% linen. We stock 20 shades and can piece-dye to Pantone TCX from 300 m.
imageAlt: Macro detail of sage linen-cotton blend fabric

faqs.question: Does a linen-cotton blend still crease?
faqs.answer: Less than pure linen. The cotton content reduces creasing noticeably, though it is not wrinkle-free. Brands wanting a crisp finish usually add a resin-free press at the laundry rather than a chemical finish.

faqs.question: What is the price difference between linen and linen-cotton?
faqs.answer: Linen-cotton typically costs 30–35% less than 100% European flax linen at the same weight, mainly because cotton fibre and its spinning route are cheaper.

name: Heavy Linen 260
summary: A 260 gsm heavyweight washed linen for structured dresses, outerwear and home textiles, with a dense hand and under 4% shrinkage, from 500 m.
description: At 260 gsm this linen carries structure: it stands away from the body, holds a pleat and works for sleeveless dresses, soft jackets and heavier home textiles. It is woven from the same certified European flax as our lighter qualities, with a denser sett.

Finishing uses a longer stone-free wash cycle to soften the heavier cloth without breaking the yarn surface. If you need a fully opaque result for unlined styles, ask for the double-washed version, which reduces light transmission by roughly 30%.
imageAlt: Macro detail of heavy rust linen fabric with structured folds

faqs.question: Is 260 gsm linen too heavy for dresses?
faqs.answer: Not for structured silhouettes. It suits sleeveless dresses, pinafores and soft tailoring. For fluid, gathered dresses choose 180 gsm instead.

faqs.question: Can heavy linen be used for upholstery?
faqs.answer: It can be used for cushions and light domestic upholstery, but for contract upholstery we recommend a Martindale-tested blend with a higher abrasion rating.

name: Rigid Denim 12.5 oz
summary: A 12.5 oz rigid indigo denim woven on shuttle looms with rope-dyed yarns, giving authentic fades for five-pocket jeans, from 500 m per shade.
description: This 12.5 oz denim uses rope-dyed indigo warp yarns and natural weft, woven on shuttle looms at 76 cm loomstate width. The rope dyeing leaves the yarn core white, which is what produces the high-contrast fade pattern denim wearers look for.

It is sanforised to 2–3% residual shrinkage, so it can be cut without a wash-first step. If your laundry runs laser or ozone finishing, tell us the recipe — we adjust the singeing and skewing to suit.
imageAlt: Macro detail of raw indigo denim with visible twill

faqs.question: What does 12.5 oz denim weigh in gsm?
faqs.answer: 12.5 oz per square yard is approximately 424 gsm. It is a mid-heavyweight denim suited to year-round five-pocket jeans and light jackets.

faqs.question: Is this denim sanforised?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is sanforised to 2–3% residual shrinkage, so it can be cut without pre-washing. Unsanforised loomstate is available on request for raw-denim programmes.

name: Stretch Denim 10 oz
summary: A 10 oz dual-core stretch denim with 1.5% elastane, tested for growth and recovery, for comfort-fit jeans and jackets from 500 m.
description: Built on dual-core yarn, this 10 oz denim stretches and recovers rather than bagging at the knee. Elastane content is 1.5%, which gives roughly 22% elongation at 10 kg load with 95% recovery after five cycles — the range most comfort-fit programmes specify.

It is finished with a low-temperature sanforising route that protects the elastane, and we report growth and recovery figures with each lot. For high-stretch skinny fits, ask about the 8 oz version with 2% elastane.
features: Growth and recovery report per lot
imageAlt: Macro detail of mid-blue stretch denim fabric

faqs.question: How much stretch does 1.5% elastane give?
faqs.answer: Around 22% elongation at 10 kg load, with about 95% recovery after five stretch cycles. That is enough for comfort-fit jeans without the rubbery hand of 3% stretch.

faqs.question: Will stretch denim lose shape after washing?
faqs.answer: Dual-core yarn limits growth to under 2% after 20 home launderings in our testing. Recovery reports are supplied with each lot so you can verify against your own wash standard.

name: Chambray 140
summary: A 140 gsm yarn-dyed chambray with indigo warp and white weft, lightweight enough for shirting and dresses, from 300 m in 12 shades.
description: Chambray uses the same indigo warp and white weft idea as denim but in a plain weave at 140 gsm, which makes it soft, breathable and light enough for shirts. The yarn-dyed construction means the colour is in the yarn, so it fades gently rather than crocking.
It is a strong seller for summer shirting and lightweight dresses, and it prints well for capsule collections. We stock 12 indigo and washed-blue shades and can match additional shades at 500 m.
imageAlt: Macro detail of light blue yarn-dyed chambray fabric

faqs.question: What is the difference between chambray and denim?
faqs.answer: Both use indigo warp and white weft, but chambray is a lightweight plain weave at 100–160 gsm while denim is a heavier twill at 300 gsm and above. Chambray is for shirting; denim is for jeans and jackets.

faqs.question: Does chambray bleed colour?
faqs.answer: Yarn-dyed chambray has low crocking and will not bleed onto adjacent fabrics in normal wear. We still recommend a cold first wash and testing against white trims in your wash standard.

name: Single Jersey 160
summary: A 160 gsm combed cotton single jersey with a compacted finish and under 5% spirality, the standard base for T-shirts and loungewear from 300 m.
description: Knitted on 34-inch circular machines from 30s combed cotton, this jersey is compacted after dyeing so it arrives close to final dimensions. Spirality is held under 5%, which matters for side-seam tees and all-over prints.
It is available in tubular or open width, with a soft or dry hand finish. For print programmes we recommend the semi-bleached base, which gives better ink yield and cleaner whites.
imageAlt: Macro detail of white cotton single jersey knit fabric

faqs.question: What is the best gsm for a T-shirt?
faqs.answer: 160–180 gsm single jersey is the standard for retail T-shirts: opaque enough not to show through, light enough to drape. Heavyweight 220–240 gsm jersey is used for boxy, structured fits.

faqs.question: Do you supply tubular knit fabric?
faqs.answer: Yes, both tubular and open width are available. Tubular is common for T-shirt programmes that cut on the tube and avoid side seams.

name: French Terry 280
summary: A 280 gsm cotton-rich French terry for hoodies and sweatshirts, with a looped back, low shrinkage and GRS recycled options, from 300 m.
description: French terry 280 is a double-knit with fine loops on the back, which gives warmth and structure without the bulk of fleece. At 280 gsm it holds a hood shape and a dropped shoulder, making it the base for most premium sweatshirt programmes.

We knit in 80/20 cotton-polyester for stability, or 100% cotton where a fully natural base is required. Shrinkage is held under 5% after three washes, and we can add an anti-pilling enzyme finish for a smoother surface.
imageAlt: Macro detail of heather grey French terry fabric

faqs.question: Is 280 gsm French terry warm enough for a hoodie?
faqs.answer: Yes for mid-season hoodies and year-round in most markets. For winter-weight hoodies with a brushed interior, choose 320–340 gsm fleece-backed terry.

faqs.question: Can French terry be garment dyed?
faqs.answer: Yes. We supply a greige base for garment dyeing and can pre-test shrinkage after your dye cycle. Garment-dyed terry typically shrinks 6–8%, so plan the pattern allowance accordingly.

name: 2x2 Rib Knit 240
summary: A 240 gsm 2x2 cotton rib with 60% width stretch for cuffs, collars and fitted tops, dyed to match our jersey and terry ranges, from 300 m.
description: This 2x2 rib is knitted to match our single jersey and French terry shade cards, so trims and bodies come out of the same dye lot family. At 240 gsm it has enough body for waistbands and cuffs without rolling.

Stretch is around 60% across the width with 90% recovery, which keeps cuffs snug after washing. Order it with the body fabric and we will dye both in the same lot to avoid shade drift on the finished garment.
features: Dyed to match jersey and terry
Narrow 120 cm width for trim cutting
imageAlt: Macro detail of cream 2x2 rib knit fabric

faqs.question: Can rib be dyed the same shade as jersey?
faqs.answer: Yes. Order rib with your body fabric and we dye both in the same lot. Because rib and jersey take dye slightly differently, same-lot dyeing is the only reliable way to avoid visible shade differences at the cuff.

faqs.question: What is 2x2 rib used for?
faqs.answer: It is used for cuffs, collars, waistbands and hems because the alternating knit and purl columns give strong crosswise stretch with good recovery. Heavier weights are also used for fitted tops and dresses.

name: Viscose Challis 110
summary: A 110 gsm viscose challis with a fluid drape and matte finish, print-ready for dresses and modest wear, from 300 m with OEKO-TEX certification.
description: Challis is a soft, loosely woven plain-weave viscose that falls in fluid folds and prints with high colour yield. At 110 gsm it is light without being sheer in mid and dark shades, which is why it dominates summer dress and abaya programmes.

We finish with a tensionless wash to remove loom tension, then test shrinkage after hand wash and dry clean. Digital reactive printing is available from 100 m so capsule collections can be produced without a rotary setup cost.
imageAlt: Macro detail of soft terracotta viscose challis fabric

faqs.question: Is viscose challis see-through?
faqs.answer: At 110 gsm it is semi-opaque in pale shades and opaque in mid to dark tones. For unlined pale dresses we recommend 130–150 gsm or a lining.

faqs.question: Can you print small runs on viscose?
faqs.answer: Yes. Digital reactive printing starts at 100 metres, which suits capsule collections. Rotary printing becomes cheaper above roughly 1,000 metres per design.

name: Viscose Linen 150
summary: A 150 gsm viscose-linen blend combining linen texture with viscose drape, low-crease and breathable for hot climates, from 300 m.
description: This blend pairs 55% viscose with 45% linen: the linen gives surface texture and breathability, the viscose gives drape and reduces creasing. At 150 gsm it works for wide-leg trousers, dresses and relaxed shirts.
Because both fibres absorb moisture well, it performs in Gulf and Mediterranean summer conditions where polyester blends feel clammy. We stock 16 shades and can dye to Pantone TCX at 300 m.
imageAlt: Macro detail of sand viscose-linen blend fabric

faqs.question: Is viscose-linen suitable for hot weather?
faqs.answer: Yes. Both fibres absorb moisture and release it quickly, and the open weave allows airflow. It is cooler than polyester blends and creases less than pure linen.

faqs.question: How should viscose-linen be washed?
faqs.answer: Cool machine wash at 30°C, low spin, hang dry away from direct sun. We test shrinkage to that method and report the result per lot.

name: Crepe Viscose 135
summary: A 135 gsm crepe viscose with a subtle grained surface and bounce, for tailored dresses, blouses and occasionwear, from 300 m.
description: Crepe viscose is woven with high-twist yarns, which gives the cloth its fine grain and a slight bounce that resists clinging. It presses cleanly, holds a soft pleat and drapes without collapsing — useful for occasionwear and tailored dresses.
At 135 gsm it is substantial enough for unlined dresses in mid tones. We finish with a gentle wash that stabilises the twist, and test for seam slippage so you can choose the right stitch density.
imageAlt: Macro detail of forest green crepe viscose fabric

faqs.question: What is crepe viscose used for?
faqs.answer: Occasionwear, blouses and tailored dresses. The high-twist yarn gives a dry, grainy hand that resists clinging and holds a soft pleat better than plain challis.

faqs.question: Does crepe viscose fray when cut?
faqs.answer: It frays moderately, more than jersey but less than loose challis. We test seam slippage per lot and can recommend stitch density and overlock settings.

name: Recycled Polyester Twill 180
summary: A 180 gsm GRS-certified recycled polyester twill with PFC-free DWR, for outerwear, bags and uniform shells, supplied with transaction certificates from 300 m.
description: This 180 gsm twill is woven from GRS-certified recycled polyester filament yarn, then finished with C0 PFC-free durable water repellency. It is the workhorse for lightweight shells, bag bodies and uniform outerwear where recycled content must be documented.

Every shipment includes a GRS transaction certificate that traces the yarn lot through to delivered metres. If your brand requires bluesign-approved chemistry, we can switch the finish recipe without changing the base cloth.
imageAlt: Water beading on deep olive recycled polyester twill

faqs.question: What does GRS certification cover?
faqs.answer: GRS 4.0 verifies recycled content, chain of custody, social and environmental practice, and chemical restrictions. Each shipment comes with a transaction certificate linking the certified yarn to the delivered fabric.

faqs.question: How long does PFC-free DWR last?
faqs.answer: Our C0 finish holds a spray rating of 4–5 through 20 home launderings. For garments needing longer performance, ask about a 30-wash recipe at a small cost premium.

name: Recycled Nylon Taslan 120
summary: A 120 gsm GRS recycled nylon taslan with a dry, papery hand for lightweight shells, windbreakers and packable jackets, from 300 m.
description: Taslan is a textured nylon with a dry, slightly papery hand and a matte surface — the classic shell fabric for packable jackets and windbreakers. At 120 gsm it packs small while staying tear-resistant.

We weave it from GRS-certified recycled nylon and finish with C0 DWR. It is down-proof enough for light quilted linings when calendered; specify the calender pass if you plan to use it as a shell over down.
imageAlt: Macro detail of matte black recycled nylon taslan fabric

faqs.question: What is taslan fabric used for?
faqs.answer: Lightweight shells, windbreakers and packable jackets. Its textured filament yarn gives a dry, papery hand and good tear resistance at low weight.

faqs.question: Is taslan waterproof?
faqs.answer: Standard taslan is water-repellent, not waterproof. For waterproof shells, specify a laminated or coated version with a hydrostatic head rating.

name: 3-Layer Softshell 320
summary: A 320 gsm 3-layer softshell with a TPU membrane rated to 10,000 mm waterproof and 5,000 g breathability, for ski, cycling and workwear programmes from 500 m.
description: This bonded 3-layer construction pairs a recycled polyester twill face, a TPU membrane and a light grid backer. It is waterproof to 10,000 mm, breathable to 5,000 g/m²/24h, and stretchy enough for articulated sleeves without a separate lining.
Bonding is done in-house with a solvent-free adhesive, and we test peel strength plus hydrostatic head on every lot. For workwear, ask about the EN 343 option with sealed-seam tape supply.
composition: Face 100% recycled polyester, TPU membrane, polyester backer
imageAlt: Macro detail of charcoal 3-layer softshell showing bonded layers

faqs.question: What does 10,000 mm waterproof mean?
faqs.answer: It is the hydrostatic head: the fabric resists a 10-metre column of water before leaking. That suits rain and snow sports, while 20,000 mm is used for expedition shells.

faqs.question: Can you supply seam tape with the softshell?
faqs.answer: Yes. Matching 20 mm seam tape is available, and for workwear we can quote an EN 343 tested package including tape and test reports.
